preview_text.Prew04: Your baby is the size of an apple seed and settling into the lining of your womb.
preview_text.Prew05: Your baby is the size of a black peppercorn. Time to get in touch with a midwife.
preview_text.Prew06: Your baby is the size of a pea, and morning sickness may be starting to show up.
preview_text.Prew07: Their brain is growing fast, and you might be feeling more tired than ever.
preview_text.Prew08: Your baby is the size of an olive and starting to make little movements.
preview_text.Prew09: Your baby is raspberry-sized and their face is becoming more defined.
preview_text.Prew10: Your baby is the size of a strawberry, and their vital organs have now formed.
preview_text.Prew11: Your baby is the size of an apricot and getting more active by the day.
preview_text.Prew12: Your baby is fig-sized, and the first trimester is nearly behind you.

preview_text.Prew14: Your baby is the size of a lemon and practising squints, frowns and grimaces.

preview_text.Prew17: Your baby is avocado-sized and starting to store fat to keep warm.
preview_text.Prew18: Your baby is the size of an onion and starting to hear sounds.
preview_text.Prew19: Your baby is pomegranate-sized and has a creamy coating to protect their skin.
preview_text.Prew20: Your baby is the size of a beef tomato, and you've reached the halfway point.
preview_text.Prew21: Your baby is pepper-sized and their movements are becoming easier to feel.
preview_text.Prew22: Your baby is the size of a sweet potato and exploring with their hands.

preview_text.Prew24: Your baby is the size of a papaya and their lungs are developing fast.
preview_text.Prew25: Your baby is grapefruit-sized and putting on weight, looking less wrinkly by the day.

preview_text.Prew27: Your baby is broccoli-sized and their brain is very busy.
preview_text.Prew28: Your baby is the size of a cantaloupe melon, and their eyes can now open and close.

copy.Prew04: Your baby has settled into the lining of your womb. Their cells are now forming layers that will become the brain, heart, skin, bones and organs.
copy.Prew05: Your baby's heart is starting to form, along with the neural tube that will become their brain and spinal cord. This is why folic acid matters so much right now.
copy.Prew06: Your baby's heart has started beating, and tiny buds are appearing that will grow into arms and legs. Their face is beginning to take shape too.
copy.Prew07: Your baby's brain is growing rapidly, and their arm buds are forming tiny hands. Their liver is busy making red blood cells until their bone marrow takes over.
copy.Prew08: Your baby's fingers and toes are forming, though they're still webbed for now. They've started making small, jerky movements, even though you won't feel them yet.
copy.Prew09: Your baby is starting to look more like a baby. Their eyelids are forming, the tip of their nose is visible and tiny earlobes are beginning to appear.
copy.Prew10: All of your baby's vital organs are now in place and starting to work. Tiny nails are forming on their fingers, and their bones are beginning to harden.
copy.Prew11: Your baby can now stretch, kick and even hiccup, though you won't feel it yet. Their hands can open and close, and tooth buds are forming in their gums.
copy.Prew12: Your baby's reflexes are developing, so they may curl their toes or squirm if your tummy is prodded. Their kidneys are working and they're now passing urine.
copy.Prew13: Your baby's fingerprints are forming on their tiny fingertips, and their vocal cords are developing. Their intestines are moving from the umbilical cord into their tummy.
copy.Prew14: Your baby's facial muscles are working, so they can squint, frown and grimace. Fine, soft hair called lanugo is starting to cover their body to help keep them warm.
copy.Prew15: Your baby can now sense light through their closed eyelids. Their legs are growing longer than their arms, and their tiny bones are getting stronger every day.
copy.Prew16: Your baby's movements are becoming more coordinated, and some people start feeling first flutters around now. Their eyes can also make small side-to-side movements.
copy.Prew17: Your baby is starting to lay down fat under their skin, which will help keep them warm after birth. Their skeleton is changing from soft cartilage to bone.
copy.Prew18: Your baby's ears are now in their final position, and they may start to hear sounds like your heartbeat and voice. Their nervous system is maturing quickly.
copy.Prew19: A creamy coating called vernix is forming on your baby's skin to protect it from the amniotic fluid. Their senses of taste, touch and smell are developing.
copy.Prew20: Your baby is now measured from head to heel, rather than head to bottom. They're swallowing amniotic fluid, which is good practice for their digestive system.
copy.Prew21: Your baby's movements are getting stronger, and you may start feeling regular kicks. Their eyebrows and eyelids are fully formed, and their bone marrow is making blood cells.
copy.Prew22: Your baby is exploring through touch, grasping the umbilical cord and stroking their face. Their lips and eyes are more defined, and their pancreas is developing.
copy.Prew23: Your baby is making breathing movements to practise for life outside the womb. Blood vessels in their lungs are developing, and their skin is still thin and see-through.
copy.Prew24: Your baby's lungs are developing the cells that make surfactant, which will help them breathe after birth. Their face is almost fully formed, with eyelashes and eyebrows.
copy.Prew25: Your baby is putting on weight, so their skin is starting to smooth out. Their hair is growing and may already have its colour and texture.
copy.Prew26: Your baby's eyes are finishing developing and will soon start to open. They're responding to sounds, and their movements may change when they hear a familiar voice.
copy.Prew27: Your baby's brain is very active, and they're sleeping and waking at regular times. They may also get hiccups, which feel like small, rhythmic jolts in your bump.
copy.Prew28: At around 37cm long and weighing around 1kg, your baby's eyes can now open and close, and their little ears can recognise the sound of your voice.
copy.Prew29: Your baby is gaining weight quickly as fat builds up under their skin. Their muscles and lungs are maturing, and their head is growing to make room for their brain.
copy.Prew30: Your baby's brain is growing quickly, and the soft hair covering their body is starting to disappear. Their bone marrow has now taken over making red blood cells.
copy.Prew31: Your baby can now turn their head from side to side, and all five senses are working. Their arms, legs and body are filling out with fat.
copy.Prew32: Your baby may be starting to settle head down, ready for birth. Their fingernails and toenails have grown, and they're practising breathing and sucking.
copy.Prew33: Your baby's bones are hardening, except their skull, which stays soft so it can move during birth. Their immune system is developing, with antibodies passing from you.
copy.Prew34: Your baby's lungs and nervous system are continuing to mature. Babies born from now usually do well, though some may need a little extra care at first.
copy.Prew35: Your baby is running out of room, so you may feel more rolls and stretches than kicks. Their kidneys are fully developed, and their liver can process some waste.
copy.Prew36: Your baby may move lower into your pelvis, ready for birth. They're shedding most of the soft hair that covered their body and swallowing it with the amniotic fluid.
copy.Prew37: Your baby is now considered full term. Their organs are ready to work on their own, and they're practising gripping, sucking, blinking and turning towards light.
copy.Prew38: Your baby has a firm grip and is building fat to help control their temperature after birth. Most of the vernix and soft hair on their skin has gone.
copy.Prew39: Your baby is fully developed and ready to be born. Their brain is still growing quickly, and their lungs are making more surfactant to help them take their first breath.
copy.Prew40: Your baby is ready to meet you. Only around 1 in 20 babies arrive on their due date, so don't worry if yours takes a little longer.

title.Prew39: When to call your maternity unit

copy.Prew04: Your body is now making hCG, the hormone a pregnancy test picks up, so you may get a positive result around when your period is due. Tender breasts, tiredness and Frequent weeing are common early signs.
copy.Prew05: Once you've had a positive test, you can refer yourself to a midwife or contact your GP surgery. Your booking appointment usually happens by week 10. Nausea, tiredness and a metallic taste may start around now.
copy.Prew06: Despite the name, morning sickness can happen at any time of day. Eating little and often, keeping plain snacks nearby and sipping cold drinks may help. If you can't keep food or fluids down, speak to your midwife or GP.
copy.Prew07: Your body is working hard to build the placenta, and rising hormone levels can leave you exhausted. Rest when you can, accept offers of help and go easy on yourself. This tiredness often eases in the second trimester.
copy.Prew08: Your booking appointment with a midwife usually takes place between weeks 8 and 10. You'll talk about your health, have some blood tests and get your maternity notes. It's a good time to ask anything on your mind.
copy.Prew09: Hormones, tiredness and nausea can all affect your mood. Feeling happy one minute and tearful the next is common in early pregnancy. Talk to someone you trust, and tell your midwife if low feelings won't lift.
copy.Prew10: Your blood volume is rising to support your baby, which can make you feel warm or light-headed, and your veins may look more visible. Stand up slowly, drink plenty of water and keep healthy snacks handy.
copy.Prew11: Your first scan is usually offered between 10 and 14 weeks. It checks your baby's growth and gives you a more accurate due date. You may also be offered screening tests, and it's your choice whether to have them.
copy.Prew12: Many people share their news after the 12-week scan, but there's no right or wrong time. Your nausea may begin to ease soon and your energy should start to return. You might notice a small bump appearing.
copy.Prew13: The second trimester is often the most comfortable stage of pregnancy. Nausea tends to fade and energy returns. You may notice more vaginal discharge, which is normal if it's clear or white with no strong smell.
copy.Prew14: With nausea easing, you may feel hungrier. You don't need extra calories until the last trimester, so focus on balanced meals with fruit, vegetables, protein and wholegrains. Keep taking a daily vitamin D supplement too.
copy.Prew15: Higher hormone levels and extra blood flow can make the lining of your nose swell, causing congestion and nosebleeds. Steam and saline drops may help. Your gums may also bleed more easily, so keep brushing gently.
copy.Prew16: You'll usually see your midwife around now to go through your scan and blood test results. You'll also be offered the whooping cough vaccine from 16 weeks, which helps protect your baby in their first weeks.
copy.Prew17: As your bump grows, lying on your back may feel uncomfortable. From 28 weeks, going to sleep on your side is recommended, so it can help to get used to it now. A pillow between your knees can make it comfier.
copy.Prew18: Your mid-pregnancy scan is usually offered between 18 and 21 weeks. The sonographer checks how your baby is developing. You may be able to find out the sex if you'd like, though not every hospital offers this.
copy.Prew19: You might notice darker patches on your face, a dark line down your tummy or darker nipples. These changes are caused by hormones and usually fade after birth. Wearing sun cream can stop patches getting darker.
copy.Prew20: From 20 weeks, your midwife can give you a MATB1 form, which you'll need to claim maternity pay. You need to tell your employer you're pregnant by week 25, along with when you'd like your leave to start.
copy.Prew21: Every baby has their own pattern of movements. Over the coming weeks, get to know what's normal for yours. If you ever notice movements slowing down or changing, contact your maternity unit straight away.
copy.Prew22: Painful cramps in your calves or feet are common, especially at night. Stretching and moving your legs and feet during the day can help. Regular gentle exercise, like walking or swimming, may help prevent them too.
copy.Prew23: Extra fluid can make your feet, ankles and fingers swell, especially later in the day. Put your feet up when you can. Sudden swelling in your face, hands or feet should be checked by your midwife urgently.
copy.Prew24: Some people are offered a glucose tolerance test between 24 and 28 weeks to check for gestational diabetes. Your midwife will let you know if you need one. It involves a sugary drink and a couple of blood tests.
copy.Prew25: An uncomfortable urge to move your legs, especially in the evening, is common in pregnancy. Gentle stretching, a warm bath or a leg massage before bed may help. Tell your midwife or GP if it's affecting your sleep.
copy.Prew26: As your womb grows, it pushes on your stomach, which can cause heartburn. Try smaller meals, avoid eating just before bed and prop yourself up with pillows. Ask your pharmacist or midwife about remedies that are safe in pregnancy.
copy.Prew27: Pregnancy hormones loosen your ligaments, which can lead to pain at the front or back of your pelvis, known as pelvic girdle pain. Tell your midwife if it's affecting you, as a physiotherapist can help.
copy.Prew28: This week your baby's brain is developing rapidly, and you might be feeling it. Third trimester tiredness is real. Your centre of gravity is shifting, back ache may be creeping in, and those Braxton Hicks contractions? Completely normal at week 28.
copy.Prew29: Your growing womb is pushing up against your diaphragm, so you may feel out of breath more easily. Slow down, sit up straight and take the stairs gently. Contact your midwife or GP if breathlessness comes on suddenly.
copy.Prew30: Now is a good time to think about where you'd like to give birth and which pain relief options appeal. A birth plan helps your midwife understand your wishes, but try to stay flexible as things can change on the day.
copy.Prew31: You may notice a yellowish fluid called colostrum leaking from your nipples. This is your body's first milk, and it's full of goodness for your newborn. Breast pads can help if leaks are bothering you.
copy.Prew32: It's a good idea to have your hospital bag ready a few weeks before your due date. Pack comfy clothes, toiletries, maternity pads, snacks and your notes, plus clothes, nappies and a car seat for your baby.
copy.Prew33: Between a busy bladder, heartburn and a growing bump, getting comfortable at night can be tricky. Try sleeping on your side with a pillow under your bump, cut back on drinks before bed and rest in the day when you can.
copy.Prew34: It's worth knowing the signs of labour now: regular, tightening contractions, your waters breaking, a 'show' of mucus or a backache that comes and goes. If you think labour has started, call your maternity unit.
copy.Prew35: Your baby should keep moving right up to and during labour. Movements may feel different as space gets tight, but they shouldn't slow down. If you notice a change, contact your maternity unit straight away.
copy.Prew36: If your baby moves down into your pelvis, you may find breathing and eating easier, but you'll probably need to wee more often. Your midwife will check your baby's position at your 36-week appointment.
copy.Prew37: You may notice more Braxton Hicks, a heavier feeling in your pelvis or losing your mucus plug. These are signs your body is preparing for labour. Keep your hospital bag by the door and your maternity unit's number handy.
copy.Prew38: The final weeks can feel long. Rest when you can, keep gently active and eat little and often to keep your energy up. It's normal to feel a mix of excitement and nerves, and your midwife is there for any worries.
copy.Prew39: Call your maternity unit if your waters break, contractions become regular and strong, you have any bleeding or your baby's movements change. Trust your instincts. If something doesn't feel right, it's always okay to call.
copy.Prew40: If you go past your due date, your midwife may offer a membrane sweep to help start labour. If labour still hasn't begun, you'll be offered an induction. Keep an eye on your baby's movements and call if anything changes.
